use.text: Pick a year where existing values jumped or fell: the rate moved the other way by about as much. Then look at development: the rate barely notices it.

paragraphs.text: The town decides the total it raises in property tax, up to a limit that grows 2.5% a year plus the tax on new construction, plus any override or debt exclusion voters approve.
The tax rate is that total divided by the value of everything taxed.
A bill is the home’s assessed value times the rate: its share of the town’s total. What the town raises sets the bill; what homes are worth only decides who pays which part of it.

why.text: The limit grows 2.5% every year, and a town may levy up to it.
Raise the limit for good, and every 2.5% after is figured on the higher total.
Add a building’s debt payments to the levy until the debt is paid off.
A town that levied below its limit can use the room without a vote.
New homes and businesses are taxed at last year’s rate; they add to the total without raising anyone else’s bill. They do raise the average bill.
The limit does not fall when property leaves or loses value, so everyone else pays its share.
Your share of the total rises with your home’s share of the town’s value.
Rising or falling across town, the rate moves the other way; the total, and so the bill, does not.

so.text: Only overrides and exclusions need a vote. Most of what raises a bill does not.

paragraphs.text: New growth by kind: new homes, additions and renovations, and businesses. The state’s files print one figure.
A real home. The unchanged home is ours, built from town-wide values; no parcel’s own assessment history has been checked against it. A home that gained on others pays more.
Our existing-value line also absorbs revaluation, abatements and class shifts, which the state’s files do not separate from market change.

blocks.title: What this page does not separate

paragraphs.text: **The average bill** is every single-family home’s tax added up, divided by the number of homes. **One home’s bill** is that home’s value times the rate.
They move differently. A new or enlarged home pays its own tax, and no other home’s bill rises. But it usually pays more than the average, so the average goes up.
The first chart draws both. The breakdown under it follows **one home’s bill**, then adds what newer homes do to **the average bill**.
